books.section: The Election of 1896 and the “Cross of Gold” Speech
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text: In 1896, William Jennings Bryan won the Democratic presidential nomination with his “Cross of Gold” speech calling for the free coinage of silver, and the People’s Party also nominated him. The Republican William McKinley, who stood for the gold standard, campaigned from his front porch in Canton, Ohio, receiving visitors instead of traveling. His campaign manager, Mark Hanna, raised far more money than Bryan’s campaign spent. McKinley won with 51 percent of the popular vote, and Republicans went on to dominate national politics for a generation. Every winner from 1876 through 1892 had taken less than half the popular vote. The last majority before 1896 was Grant’s in 1872.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts, grounded in Barron’s Chapter 8, Topic 6.13, and 5 Steps Chapter 18.

options.text: Receiving visitors and speaking from his home in Canton, Ohio
Traveling by train to speak in every state capital
options.misconception: McKinley stayed home; Bryan was the candidate who traveled widely.

options.text: Debating Bryan face to face in public halls
options.misconception: The two men never debated; McKinley campaigned from his porch.

options.text: Refusing to campaign at all until after election day
options.misconception: McKinley campaigned actively from home, greeting delegations daily.

rationales.A: The stimulus says McKinley received visitors at home instead of traveling.
rationales.B: Staying home was the point; Bryan did the traveling.
rationales.C: No Lincoln-Douglas style debate took place in 1896.
rationales.D: Greeting delegations from his porch was campaigning, not refusing it.
rationales.general:
Use the stimulus definition of the campaign.
1. McKinley stayed at his home in Canton, Ohio.
2. He received visiting delegations and spoke to them from his porch.
3. His manager Hanna handled money and organization elsewhere.
4. A front-porch campaign let McKinley look calm while others did the traveling.
Remember: a campaign nickname describes how the candidate ran, so use it literally.
